sections.title: Autotrophs and the leaf factory: the most important reaction on Earth

board_events.text: Photosynthesis: the Earth's food factory
Autotrophs manufacture their own food from carbon dioxide, water and sunlight, using the green pigment chlorophyll.

board_events.caption: The leaf factory: free raw materials, free power supply, green machinery

board_events.text: Site: the mesophyll cells of green leaves, packed with chloroplasts. Any green part can do a little.
Almost every food chain begins with photosynthesis. Even coal, oil and gas are sunlight captured millions of years ago.
The most important anabolic (building-up) process on the planet.
Two shifts: the light (photochemical) phase banks energy as ATP and NADPH; the biosynthetic phase spends it to build sugar.
'Dark reaction' is a misleading name. It does not need darkness; it simply does not use light directly.
Needs all four: chlorophyll, light, carbon dioxide, water. Remove any one and photosynthesis stops.

segments.text: <curious>Where does the food on your plate actually come from? Trace every samosa, every litre of petrol, every breath of oxygen far enough back, and you arrive at a green leaf.
Plants are autotrophs. They do not eat; they manufacture. Three almost free ingredients — carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil, and sunlight — plus the green pigment chlorophyll.
Picture a factory. Raw materials arrive free, the Sun is the unpaid power supply, chlorophyll is the machinery, glucose is the finished product, and oxygen leaves the chimney as clean waste.
Where does the factory sit? Chiefly in the mesophyll cells of green leaves, which are packed with chloroplasts. A young stem or a green fruit manages a little, but the leaf does the real work.
Animals, fungi, and even the non-green parts of the plant itself are all customers of this factory. Every food chain starts here, and coal, oil and gas are simply very old sunlight.

So photosynthesis is the most important anabolic process on Earth. Anabolic means building up — locking atmospheric carbon into sugar. Strip it away and the biosphere collapses within a single season.
The factory runs in two shifts. The light, or photochemical, phase captures sunlight and banks it as A T P and N A D P H. The biosynthetic phase then spends that energy building sugar.
That second shift is loosely called the dark reaction, and the name misleads students every single year. It does not need darkness at all. It simply does not use light directly.
Finally, hold on to this list: chlorophyll, light, carbon dioxide, water. All four are essential — remove any single one and the factory shuts down. The next experiment proves exactly that.
<curious>ज़रा सोचो — तुम्हारी plate का खाना आख़िर आता कहाँ से है? हर samosa, हर litre petrol, हर साँस की oxygen — पीछे जाओ तो एक green leaf मिलता है।
Plants autotrophs होते हैं। वो खाते नहीं, बनाते हैं। तीन लगभग free ingredients — hawa से carbon dioxide, mitti से water, और sunlight — और साथ में green pigment chlorophyll।
एक factory सोचो। Raw material free आता है, Sun unpaid power supply है, chlorophyll machinery है, glucose finished product है, और oxygen chimney से clean waste बनकर निकल जाती है।
Factory बैठी कहाँ है? मुख्यतः green leaves की mesophyll cells में, जो chloroplasts से भरी होती हैं। Young stem या green fruit थोड़ा-बहुत कर लेते हैं, असली काम leaf ही करता है।
Animals, fungi, और plant के अपने non-green parts — सब इसी factory के customers हैं। हर food chain यहीं से शुरू होती है, और coal, oil, gas तो बस बहुत पुरानी sunlight है।
इसलिए photosynthesis धरती की सबसे ज़रूरी anabolic process है। Anabolic यानी building up — atmospheric carbon को sugar में lock करना। ये हट जाए तो biosphere एक ही season में ख़त्म।
Factory दो shifts में चलती है। Light यानी photochemical phase sunlight पकड़कर उसे A T P और N A D P H में bank करती है। फिर biosynthetic phase उसी energy से sugar बनाती है।
दूसरी shift को ढीले तौर पर dark reaction कहते हैं, और यही नाम हर साल students को धोखा देता है। इसे अँधेरा नहीं चाहिए। ये बस light सीधे use नहीं करती।
आख़िर में ये list पकड़ लो: chlorophyll, light, carbon dioxide, water — चारों essential हैं। कोई एक हटाओ, factory बंद। अगला experiment बिलकुल यही prove करता है।

sections.title: The half-leaf experiment: proving what the factory needs

board_events.text: The half-leaf experiment
Cover half a leaf so that light or carbon dioxide cannot reach it. Leave the plant standing in sunlight.

board_events.caption: Cover one half, expose to sunlight, then test the whole leaf with iodine

board_events.text: Then test the WHOLE leaf — both halves together — with iodine.
Only the exposed half turns blue-black.
Blue-black with iodine means starch. Starch is the stored form of the glucose that region manufactured.
Conclusion: chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide are all essential for photosynthesis.
The starch test rests on Sachs' finding that glucose is stored as starch inside chloroplasts.

segments.text: A classic schoolroom demonstration settles the question of what the factory needs. It requires nothing more than a leaf, something to cover it with, and a bottle of iodine.
Take a leaf still attached to the plant and cover one half — block it so that light, or carbon dioxide, cannot reach that half. Now leave the whole plant standing in sunlight.
Notice the design. One leaf, two halves, identical in every way except for the one factor you blocked. The plant is its own control — that is exactly what makes the result so clean.
After a few hours, pluck the leaf and test all of it with iodine. Not just the exposed part — the whole leaf, both halves together, so the comparison is side by side.
The result is unmistakable. Only the exposed half turns blue-black. The covered half stays pale.
Blue-black with iodine means starch. And starch is simply the stored form of the glucose that region manufactured. So the exposed half photosynthesised, and the covered half did not.
That single colour difference proves the whole list at once: chlorophyll in the green tissue, light falling on it, and carbon dioxide reaching it. Block any one of them and no starch appears.
And the test itself rests on Sachs' discovery that green parts make glucose and store it as starch inside their chloroplasts. Without that link, the iodine bottle would tell you nothing.
एक classic schoolroom demonstration ये सवाल हमेशा के लिए settle कर देता है। इसमें बस एक leaf चाहिए, उसे ढकने के लिए कुछ, और iodine की एक शीशी।
Plant से जुड़ी हुई एक leaf लो और उसका आधा हिस्सा ढक दो — ऐसे कि उस half तक light या carbon dioxide न पहुँचे। अब पूरा plant sunlight में खड़ा रहने दो।
Design पर ध्यान दो। एक leaf, दो halves, हर तरह से identical — सिवाय उस एक factor के जो तुमने block किया। Plant ख़ुद अपना control है, इसीलिए result इतना clean आता है।
कुछ घंटों बाद leaf तोड़ो और पूरी leaf को iodine से test करो। सिर्फ़ exposed हिस्सा नहीं — दोनों halves साथ में, ताकि comparison आमने-सामने दिखे।
Result बिलकुल साफ़ है। सिर्फ़ exposed half blue-black होता है। Covered half pale ही रहता है।
Iodine के साथ blue-black का मतलब है starch। और starch उसी glucose का stored form है जो उस हिस्से ने बनाया। यानी exposed half ने photosynthesis की, covered half ने नहीं।
यही एक colour difference पूरी list prove कर देता है: green tissue में chlorophyll, उस पर पड़ती light, और वहाँ पहुँचती carbon dioxide। कोई एक block करो — starch ग़ायब।
और ये test ख़ुद Sachs की खोज पर टिका है कि green parts glucose बनाकर उसे chloroplasts के अंदर starch की तरह store करते हैं। वो link न हो तो iodine कुछ नहीं बताती।

board_events.caption: Twelve waters in, six waters out — the released oxygen traces back to water

board_events.text: Twelve water molecules go in and six come out — written this way precisely because the oxygen released comes from water, not carbon dioxide.
Glucose is the representative carbohydrate product. The equation is only a net summary — it hides dozens of real steps.
Autotroph here means photoautotroph: an organism that synthesises its own organic food from inorganic raw materials using light.
Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are photoautotrophs.
Exception: green and purple sulphur bacteria are photoautotrophs too, but they use hydrogen sulphide instead of water.
So sulphur bacteria liberate sulphur, not oxygen — a favourite examiner exception.

segments.text: Every student of this chapter must be able to write one equation cold, and must be able to read it carefully enough to spot what it is quietly telling you.
Six carbon dioxide plus twelve water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, gives one glucose, plus six oxygen, plus six water.
Now read the water. Twelve molecules go in on the left. Six come out on the right. Why bother writing it that way, when you could just cancel and write six?
Because the balance is making a point. The oxygen released does not come from the carbon dioxide the plant breathes in — it comes from the water the plant splits. Twelve in, six out is the giveaway.
Two honest caveats. Glucose is the representative carbohydrate product, standing in for the sugars a plant actually makes. And the equation is a net summary — it hides dozens of real steps inside.
Now the vocabulary. Autotroph here means photoautotroph: an organism that synthesises its own organic food from inorganic raw materials, using light as the energy source.
Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are all photoautotrophs. They take in carbon dioxide and water, they use light, and they hand oxygen back to the atmosphere.
But here is the exception examiners love. Green and purple sulphur bacteria are photoautotrophs too — yet they use hydrogen sulphide, not water, as their hydrogen donor.
<whisper>And so they liberate sulphur instead of oxygen. Remember that exception: it is not a footnote, it is the clue that unlocks van Niel's entire argument later in this subtopic.
इस chapter के हर student को एक equation बिलकुल रटी हुई आनी चाहिए — और उसे इतने ध्यान से पढ़ना आना चाहिए कि वो चुपचाप जो बता रही है, वो पकड़ में आ जाए।
Six carbon dioxide plus twelve water, light और chlorophyll की मौजूदगी में, देते हैं एक glucose, plus six oxygen, plus six water।
अब water को पढ़ो। बाईं तरफ़ बारह molecules जा रहे हैं, दाईं तरफ़ छह निकल रहे हैं। ऐसे लिखने की ज़रूरत क्या थी, cancel करके छह लिख देते?
क्योंकि ये balance एक point बना रहा है। जो oxygen निकलती है वो plant की ली हुई carbon dioxide से नहीं आती — वो उस water से आती है जिसे plant तोड़ता है। बारह अंदर, छह बाहर — यही giveaway है।
दो ईमानदार caveats। Glucose representative carbohydrate product है, बाक़ी sugars की जगह खड़ा हुआ। और ये equation सिर्फ़ net summary है — इसके अंदर दर्जनों असली steps छिपे हैं।
अब vocabulary। यहाँ autotroph का मतलब है photoautotroph: वो organism जो inorganic raw materials से, light को energy source बनाकर, अपना organic food ख़ुद बनाता है।
Green plants, algae और cyanobacteria — सब photoautotrophs हैं। ये carbon dioxide और water लेते हैं, light use करते हैं, और बदले में atmosphere को oxygen लौटाते हैं।
लेकिन यहाँ वो exception है जो examiners को बेहद पसंद है। Green और purple sulphur bacteria भी photoautotrophs हैं — मगर वो hydrogen donor के तौर पर water नहीं, hydrogen sulphide use करते हैं।
<whisper>इसलिए वो oxygen नहीं, sulphur छोड़ते हैं। ये exception याद रखो — ये footnote नहीं है, यही आगे van Niel की पूरी argument खोलने वाली चाबी है।

sections.title: The four leaf pigments and the chromatogram

board_events.text: Separating leaf pigments by paper chromatography
Grind leaf tissue in a solvent, spot the extract near one end of a paper strip, and dip that end in solvent.

board_events.caption: Four bands: chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids

board_events.text: As the solvent climbs, pigments travel at different rates by solubility and adsorption, separating into four coloured bands.
Chlorophyll a: bright or blue-green. Chlorophyll b: yellow-green.
Xanthophylls: yellow. Carotenoids (carotenes): yellow to yellow-orange.
Chief pigment: chlorophyll a — the only pigment that actually drives the light reaction at the reaction centre.
Accessory pigments: chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids.
Their three jobs: widen the range of wavelengths harvested, funnel that energy to chlorophyll a, and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

segments.text: A leaf is not green because of one pigment. It is green because of a small committee of pigments, and there is a simple bench technique that pulls that committee apart into its members.
Grind leaf tissue in a solvent so the pigments dissolve out. Spot that extract near one end of a chromatography paper strip. Dip that end — just the end — into fresh solvent.
Now watch the strip. The solvent climbs the paper by capillary action, and it drags the pigments with it. But it does not drag them equally, and that is the whole trick.
Each pigment travels at its own rate, set by how soluble it is in the running solvent and how strongly it sticks to the paper. Four separate coloured bands appear, in a fixed order.
Chlorophyll a shows up as bright or blue-green. Chlorophyll b sits as a yellow-green band. Those two are the chlorophylls, and the colour difference between them is examined constantly.
Above them, xanthophylls appear yellow, and carotenoids — the carotenes — appear yellow to yellow-orange. Reading the strip therefore tells you exactly which pigments a leaf contains.
Now the hierarchy, and this is the marks-carrying line. Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment. It is the only pigment that sits at the reaction centre and actually drives the light reaction.
The other three — chlorophyll b, the xanthophylls and the carotenoids — are accessory pigments. They do not drive the reaction themselves, but the plant would be far poorer without them.
They do three jobs. They widen the range of wavelengths the plant can harvest. They funnel that absorbed energy to chlorophyll a. And they shield chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation — sun damage.
Leaf एक pigment की वजह से हरी नहीं होती। वो pigments की एक छोटी committee की वजह से हरी होती है — और एक आसान bench technique उस committee को उसके members में तोड़ देती है।
Leaf tissue को solvent में grind करो ताकि pigments घुल जाएँ। उस extract को chromatography paper strip के एक सिरे के पास spot करो। फिर वही सिरा — सिर्फ़ सिरा — fresh solvent में डुबा दो।
अब strip देखो। Solvent capillary action से paper पर ऊपर चढ़ता है और pigments को साथ खींचता है। लेकिन सबको बराबर नहीं खींचता — और यही पूरा trick है।
हर pigment अपनी रफ़्तार से चलता है, जो तय होती है उसकी solvent में solubility और paper पर adsorption से। नतीजा — चार अलग coloured bands, एक fixed order में।
Chlorophyll a दिखता है bright या blue-green। Chlorophyll b बैठता है yellow-green band की तरह। ये दोनों chlorophylls हैं, और इनका colour difference लगातार पूछा जाता है।
उनके ऊपर xanthophylls yellow दिखते हैं, और carotenoids यानी carotenes yellow से yellow-orange। इसलिए strip पढ़ लो तो पता चल जाता है कि leaf में कौन-कौन से pigments हैं।
अब hierarchy — और यही marks वाली line है। Chlorophyll a chief pigment है। यही अकेला pigment reaction centre पर बैठता है और असल में light reaction चलाता है।
बाक़ी तीन — chlorophyll b, xanthophylls और carotenoids — accessory pigments हैं। ये ख़ुद reaction नहीं चलाते, मगर इनके बिना plant बहुत ग़रीब हो जाता।
इनके तीन काम हैं। Wavelengths की range चौड़ी करना। पकड़ी हुई energy को chlorophyll a तक funnel करना। और chlorophyll a को photo-oxidation यानी sun damage से बचाना।

board_events.caption: The two curves overlap closely — evidence that chlorophyll a drives photosynthesis

board_events.text: Chlorophyll a absorbs most strongly in the blue (~430 nm) and red (~660 nm) regions, and least in the green.
Leaves look green because chlorophyll REFLECTS green — not because it absorbs it.
Action spectrum: a graph of how fast photosynthesis itself proceeds at each wavelength.
Its peaks line up closely with chlorophyll a's absorption peaks.
That close overlap confirms chlorophyll a is the main pigment responsible. Blue and red are most effective; green is least.

segments.text: Two graphs sit at the heart of this subtopic, they look almost identical when drawn, and students mix them up in the exam hall every single year. Let us separate them properly.
The first is the absorption spectrum. Take one pigment, shine each wavelength at it in turn, and plot how much light it soaks up. This graph is about a pigment, not about photosynthesis.
For chlorophyll a the curve has two humps and a deep valley between them. Both humps and the valley carry meaning, and both are examined.
The humps sit in the blue, near four hundred thirty nanometres, and in the red, near six hundred sixty nanometres. The valley sits in the green — chlorophyll a absorbs green very poorly.
And that valley explains something you have seen your whole life. Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light back at your eye. It is not absorbing green — it is rejecting it.
Now the second graph, the action spectrum. Here you shine each wavelength and plot how fast photosynthesis actually proceeds. This graph is about the process, not about any one pigment.
And here is the beautiful result. The action peaks line up closely with chlorophyll a's absorption peaks. Where chlorophyll a absorbs hardest, photosynthesis runs fastest.
That overlap is evidence, not coincidence. It confirms that chlorophyll a is the main pigment responsible. Blue and red light are most effective; green light is the least effective of all.
इस subtopic के केंद्र में दो graphs हैं, बने हुए दोनों लगभग एक जैसे दिखते हैं, और students हर साल exam hall में इन्हें आपस में गड्डमड्ड कर देते हैं। इन्हें ठीक से अलग करते हैं।
पहला है absorption spectrum। एक pigment लो, उस पर बारी-बारी हर wavelength डालो, और plot करो कि वो कितनी light सोखता है। ये graph pigment के बारे में है, photosynthesis के बारे में नहीं।
Chlorophyll a के लिए curve में दो humps हैं और बीच में एक गहरी valley। दोनों humps और वो valley — तीनों meaning रखते हैं, और तीनों पूछे जाते हैं।
Humps बैठते हैं blue में, चार सौ तीस nanometres के आसपास, और red में, छह सौ साठ के आसपास। Valley बैठती है green में — chlorophyll a green बहुत कम absorb करता है।

और यही valley वो चीज़ समझाती है जो तुमने ज़िंदगी भर देखी है। Leaves हरी इसलिए दिखती हैं क्योंकि chlorophyll green light वापस तुम्हारी आँख की तरफ़ reflect करता है। वो green सोख नहीं रहा — ठुकरा रहा है।
अब दूसरा graph — action spectrum। यहाँ हर wavelength डालकर plot करते हैं कि photosynthesis असल में कितनी तेज़ चल रही है। ये graph process के बारे में है, किसी एक pigment के बारे में नहीं।
और यहाँ नतीजा बेहद ख़ूबसूरत है। Action के peaks chlorophyll a के absorption peaks से क़रीब-क़रीब मेल खाते हैं। जहाँ chlorophyll a सबसे ज़्यादा सोखता है, वहीं photosynthesis सबसे तेज़ चलती है।
ये overlap इत्तेफ़ाक़ नहीं, evidence है। यही confirm करता है कि chlorophyll a मुख्य pigment है। Blue और red सबसे effective, और green सबसे कम effective।

board_events.text: But with a sprig of mint kept in the jar for a few days, the air was restored: a candle burned again and a mouse could live.
Conclusion: plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove — the first hint that plants release oxygen.
Priestley did not yet know the process required light.
Ingenhousz: the effect works only in sunlight, and only the green parts of a plant do it.
He saw tiny oxygen bubbles forming around the green portions of a submerged plant in light — never in the dark, never around non-green parts.

segments.text: The scientists in this subtopic are not decoration. Each one added exactly one brick to the wall, and examiners test whether you know which brick belongs to whom. Start in the seventeen seventies, with Priestley.
Priestley sealed a burning candle inside a bell jar. The flame soon went out. Something about the trapped air had been used up — spoiled, in his language. A mouse placed in that same air suffocated.
Look at the three jars carefully. Candle alone, flame dies. Mouse alone, mouse distressed. But the third jar is where the discovery lives.
Into that third jar he put a sprig of mint and left it for a few days. The air came back to life. A candle would burn in it again, and a mouse could live in it.
His conclusion was simple and enormous: plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove. That is the first hint in history that plants release oxygen.
But notice what Priestley did not know. He had no idea the process required light. His mint sprig was quietly using sunlight the whole time, and he never made that connection.
Ingenhousz made it. He showed Priestley's effect works only in sunlight — and that only the green parts of a plant can do it. Two refinements, one name.
His evidence was direct. He watched tiny oxygen bubbles form around the green portions of a submerged plant in the light. In the dark, no bubbles. Around non-green parts, no bubbles.
इस subtopic के scientists सजावट नहीं हैं। हर एक ने दीवार में ठीक एक ईंट जोड़ी, और examiners यही टेस्ट करते हैं कि कौन-सी ईंट किसकी है। शुरुआत सत्रह सौ सत्तर के दशक से, Priestley के साथ।
Priestley ने एक जलती candle को bell jar में बंद कर दिया। Flame जल्दी ही बुझ गई। बंद hawa में कुछ ख़त्म हो चुका था — उनकी ज़ुबान में spoiled। उसी hawa में रखा mouse दम घुटकर मर गया।
तीनों jars ग़ौर से देखो। अकेली candle — flame बुझ जाती है। अकेला mouse — mouse परेशान। लेकिन असली खोज तीसरे jar में है।
उस तीसरे jar में उन्होंने mint की एक टहनी रखी और कुछ दिन छोड़ दिया। Hawa दोबारा ज़िंदा हो गई। उसमें candle फिर जल उठी, और mouse ज़िंदा रह सका।
उनका conclusion आसान था और ज़बरदस्त: plants hawa को वो लौटा देते हैं जो साँस लेते animals और जलती candles छीन लेते हैं। इतिहास का पहला इशारा कि plants oxygen छोड़ते हैं।
पर ध्यान दो, Priestley क्या नहीं जानते थे। उन्हें अंदाज़ा ही नहीं था कि इसके लिए light चाहिए। उनकी mint चुपचाप sunlight use कर रही थी, और वो connection उन्होंने कभी नहीं जोड़ा।
वो connection Ingenhousz ने जोड़ा। उन्होंने दिखाया कि Priestley वाला effect सिर्फ़ sunlight में चलता है — और सिर्फ़ plant के green parts ही ये कर सकते हैं। दो refinements, एक नाम।
उनका evidence सीधा था। Light में डूबे हुए plant के green हिस्सों के चारों तरफ़ उन्होंने छोटे oxygen bubbles बनते देखे। अँधेरे में bubbles नहीं। Non-green parts के पास bubbles नहीं।

sections.title: Sachs and Engelmann: starch in the chloroplast, and the first action spectrum

board_events.text: Sachs (1854): the product is glucose, stored as starch
Sachs showed the green parts of a plant produce glucose, and that glucose is usually stored as starch within their chloroplasts.
This pinned food-making down to green, chloroplast-containing tissue and identified the actual product.
It is also the basis of the iodine starch test — and therefore of the half-leaf experiment.

board_events.text: He split a beam of light with a prism and laid the spectrum along the filamentous green alga Cladophora.
Aerobic bacteria, added to the slide, swim toward the highest oxygen concentration.
They crowded in the blue and red bands — marking the wavelengths that drove the most photosynthesis. The first action spectrum.

segments.text: Priestley and Ingenhousz established that something is released. Sachs, in eighteen fifty four, answered the opposite question: what is actually made, and where does it end up?
Sachs showed that the green parts of a plant produce glucose, and that the glucose is usually stored as starch — stored right there, inside the chloroplasts of those green cells.
That was a major step for two reasons. It pinned food-making down to green, chloroplast-containing tissue, and it named the actual product instead of leaving it vague.

It also handed us a test. A region that has photosynthesised turns blue-black with iodine; a region kept in the dark or starved of carbon dioxide does not. The half-leaf experiment is built entirely on this.
Now to Engelmann, and one of the most elegant experiments in your syllabus. His question: which colours of light actually drive photosynthesis?
<excited>He needed an oxygen meter, and he did not have one. So he built one out of living things.

He took the filamentous green alga Cladophora, split a beam of white light into its colours with a prism, and laid that spectrum along the length of the filament — violet at one end, red at the other.
Then he added aerobic bacteria to the slide. Aerobic bacteria swim toward the highest oxygen concentration. So wherever the alga was releasing the most oxygen, the bacteria would gather.

And gather they did — densely under the blue band and densely under the red band, sparsely under green. The bacteria had marked the most productive wavelengths. That is the first action spectrum of photosynthesis.
Priestley और Ingenhousz ने साबित किया कि कुछ निकलता है। Sachs ने, अठारह सौ चौवन में, उल्टा सवाल हल किया: असल में बनता क्या है, और वो जाता कहाँ है?
Sachs ने दिखाया कि plant के green parts glucose बनाते हैं, और वो glucose आम तौर पर starch की शक्ल में store होता है — वहीं, उन्हीं green cells के chloroplasts के अंदर।
ये बड़ा क़दम था, दो वजहों से। इसने food-making को green, chloroplast वाले tissue पर pin कर दिया, और product को गोल-मोल छोड़ने के बजाय उसका नाम दे दिया।
इसी ने हमें एक test भी दिया। जिस हिस्से ने photosynthesis की, वो iodine से blue-black हो जाता है; अँधेरे में रखा या carbon dioxide से वंचित हिस्सा नहीं होता। Half-leaf experiment पूरा इसी पर खड़ा है।
अब चलते हैं Engelmann पर — तुम्हारे syllabus के सबसे ख़ूबसूरत experiments में से एक। उनका सवाल: light के कौन-से रंग असल में photosynthesis चलाते हैं?
<excited>उन्हें एक oxygen meter चाहिए था, और वो था नहीं। तो उन्होंने ज़िंदा चीज़ों से meter बना डाला।
उन्होंने filamentous green alga Cladophora ली, prism से white light को उसके रंगों में तोड़ा, और वो spectrum filament की लंबाई पर बिछा दिया — एक सिरे पर violet, दूसरे पर red।
फिर slide पर aerobic bacteria डाल दिए। Aerobic bacteria वहाँ तैरते हैं जहाँ oxygen सबसे ज़्यादा हो। यानी alga जहाँ सबसे ज़्यादा oxygen छोड़ रही होगी, bacteria वहीं जमा होंगे।
और वो जमा हुए भी — blue band के नीचे घने, red band के नीचे घने, green के नीचे छितरे हुए। Bacteria ने सबसे productive wavelengths mark कर दीं। यही photosynthesis का पहला action spectrum है।

board_events.text: Reasoning by analogy, he proposed the first hypothesis that in green plants the oxygen released is derived from water.
He generalised photosynthesis as a light-driven splitting of a hydrogen donor, written H2A.
$2\,H_2A + CO_2 \xrightarrow{light} 2\,A + CH_2O + H_2O$
For green plants the donor is water, so A is oxygen — neatly explaining why oxygen is the by-product.
Later isotope experiments confirmed him. This is the single most-tested point in the subtopic.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a question that looks obvious and is not. A plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen. So the oxygen must come from the carbon dioxide — surely?

Cornelius van Niel said no, and he did not prove it by studying plants. He proved it by studying bacteria — the photosynthetic sulphur bacteria that use hydrogen sulphide and deposit sulphur instead of releasing oxygen.
Look at the two panels. The bacterium splits hydrogen sulphide and drops sulphur. The plant splits water and releases oxygen. Same shape of reaction, one ingredient swapped.
That was the whole argument. Reasoning by analogy, van Niel proposed the first hypothesis that in green plants the oxygen released is derived from water — not from carbon dioxide at all.
And he made the analogy formal. He generalised photosynthesis as a light-driven splitting of a hydrogen donor, which he wrote as H two A — a placeholder for whatever the organism happens to use.
Two H two A plus carbon dioxide, driven by light, gives two A plus C H two O plus water. Put hydrogen sulphide in as the donor and A becomes sulphur. The bacterium's behaviour drops straight out.
Now put water in as the donor. A becomes oxygen. The by-product we breathe is simply the leftover half of a water molecule — and the twelve-in, six-out equation suddenly makes complete sense.
Later isotope experiments confirmed him outright. Learn this line: the oxygen comes from water. It is the most-tested point in the subtopic, and the assertion-reason trap is built on it every year.
<curious>एक सवाल जो obvious लगता है, मगर है नहीं। Plant carbon dioxide लेता है और oxygen छोड़ता है। तो oxygen carbon dioxide से ही आती होगी — है ना?

Cornelius van Niel ने कहा नहीं। और उन्होंने ये plants पढ़कर साबित नहीं किया — bacteria पढ़कर किया। वही photosynthetic sulphur bacteria जो hydrogen sulphide use करते हैं और oxygen के बजाय sulphur जमा करते हैं।
दोनों panels देखो। Bacterium hydrogen sulphide तोड़ता है और sulphur गिराता है। Plant water तोड़ता है और oxygen छोड़ता है। Reaction का shape वही, बस एक ingredient बदला हुआ।
बस यही पूरी argument थी। Analogy से सोचते हुए van Niel ने पहली hypothesis रखी कि green plants में निकलती oxygen water से आती है — carbon dioxide से बिलकुल नहीं।
और उन्होंने इस analogy को formal भी कर दिया। उन्होंने photosynthesis को hydrogen donor की light-driven splitting बताया, जिसे उन्होंने H two A लिखा — यानी जो भी donor organism use करे, उसकी जगह।
Two H two A plus carbon dioxide, light से चलकर, देते हैं two A plus C H two O plus water। Donor की जगह hydrogen sulphide रखो — A बन जाता है sulphur। Bacterium का behaviour सीधे निकल आता है।
अब donor की जगह water रखो। A बन जाती है oxygen। जिस by-product को हम साँस में लेते हैं वो बस water molecule का बचा हुआ आधा हिस्सा है — और बारह अंदर, छह बाहर वाली equation एकदम साफ़ हो जाती है।
बाद के isotope experiments ने उन्हें पूरी तरह सही ठहराया। ये line रट लो: oxygen water से आती है। यही subtopic का सबसे ज़्यादा पूछा जाने वाला point है, और हर साल assertion-reason trap इसी पर बनता है।

$6\,CO_2 + 12\,H_2O \xrightarrow{light,\ chlorophyll} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6\,O_2 + 6\,H_2O$
The oxygen released comes from water — which is why 12 H2O appear as reactants and 6 H2O as products. First proposed by van Niel.

board_events.text: Anchor the two most distinctive: Engelmann is the action spectrum (R); van Niel is oxygen from water (P). These never move.
That leaves Priestley and Ingenhousz for Q and S. Priestley's bell jar restored air (Q); Ingenhousz added the light-and-green-parts refinement (S).
Answer: Priestley-Q, Ingenhousz-S, Engelmann-R, van Niel-P. Speed tip: lock the unique pairings first; the rest fall out by elimination.

segments.text: Two worked examples, and they are the two shapes this subtopic almost always takes in a paper. The first is a clean board presentation. The second is a speed trap that rewards technique over recall.

Example one, a C B S E favourite: write the overall balanced equation of photosynthesis and state the source of the oxygen released. Here it is — six carbon dioxide plus twelve water, over light and chlorophyll, giving glucose plus six oxygen plus six water.

Now the second half of the question, which carries the marks. The oxygen released comes from water. Point at the equation as your evidence: twelve waters as reactants, six as products, and credit van Niel for the proposal.

Example two, a N E E T speed trap. Match four scientists — Priestley, Ingenhousz, Engelmann, van Niel — to four contributions labelled P, Q, R and S. Under time pressure, most students try to recall all four cold. Do not.
Read the four contributions first. P is oxygen from water. Q is restored used air. R is the first action spectrum. S is light and green parts essential. Now attack the ones that cannot possibly move.
Look at the grid. Two pairings are unique and unmistakable. Engelmann means action spectrum, so Engelmann is R. van Niel means oxygen from water, so van Niel is P. Lock those two immediately.
Why start there? Because those two names have exactly one contribution each in the whole chapter. There is no competing candidate. They cost you no thought and they remove half the question.
Now only Priestley and Ingenhousz are left, facing only Q and S. Priestley's bell jar restored the spoiled air — that is Q. Ingenhousz added the light-and-green-parts refinement — that is S.
So the answer is Priestley Q, Ingenhousz S, Engelmann R, van Niel P. And the speed tip generalises: in any matching question, lock the unique pairings first and let the rest fall out by elimination.
दो worked examples, और यही दो shapes हैं जिनमें ये subtopic लगभग हमेशा paper में आता है। पहला clean board presentation है। दूसरा speed trap है, जो recall से ज़्यादा technique को इनाम देता है।

Example one, C B S E का favourite: photosynthesis की overall balanced equation लिखो और बताओ कि निकलती oxygen का source क्या है। ये रही — six carbon dioxide plus twelve water, light और chlorophyll पर, देते हैं glucose plus six oxygen plus six water।

अब सवाल का दूसरा हिस्सा, जिसमें marks हैं। निकलती oxygen water से आती है। Evidence के तौर पर equation की तरफ़ इशारा करो: बारह waters reactants में, छह products में — और proposal का credit van Niel को दो।

Example two, एक N E E T speed trap। चार scientists — Priestley, Ingenhousz, Engelmann, van Niel — को चार contributions P, Q, R, S से match करो। Time pressure में ज़्यादातर students चारों को याद करने बैठ जाते हैं। मत बैठो।
पहले चारों contributions पढ़ो। P यानी oxygen from water। Q यानी restored used air। R यानी first action spectrum। S यानी light और green parts essential। अब उन पर हमला करो जो हिल ही नहीं सकते।
Grid देखो। दो pairings unique हैं और बिलकुल साफ़। Engelmann मतलब action spectrum, तो Engelmann is R। van Niel मतलब oxygen from water, तो van Niel is P। इन दोनों को तुरंत lock कर दो।
यहीं से क्यों शुरू करें? क्योंकि पूरे chapter में इन दो नामों के पास ठीक एक-एक contribution है। कोई competing candidate है ही नहीं। ये बिना सोचे मिल जाते हैं और आधा सवाल हटा देते हैं।
अब बचे सिर्फ़ Priestley और Ingenhousz, सामने सिर्फ़ Q और S। Priestley के bell jar ने spoiled air restore की — वो है Q। Ingenhousz ने light और green parts वाला refinement जोड़ा — वो है S।
तो answer है Priestley Q, Ingenhousz S, Engelmann R, van Niel P। और speed tip generalise होता है: किसी भी matching question में unique pairings पहले lock करो, बाक़ी elimination से ख़ुद गिर जाएँगे।

board_events.text: The four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange).
Carotenoids are least polar and most soluble in the running solvent, so they travel farthest. Answer: carotenoids, yellow-orange.
Example 4 [NEET High-Difficulty]: assertion and reason
A: In green plants, the oxygen evolved during photosynthesis comes from water.
R: Photosynthetic sulphur bacteria use hydrogen sulphide instead of water and release sulphur rather than oxygen.
Both statements are true — and R is precisely the evidence that led van Niel to A.
Answer: (a) both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

segments.text: Two more examples. The third tests whether you can read a chromatogram rather than merely recite one. The fourth is the assertion-reason item this subtopic sets almost every year.

Example three, from C U E T: arrange the four leaf pigments on a chromatogram, and give the colour of the topmost-travelling, least-polar pigment. Notice the question hands you the reasoning tool — the word 'least-polar'.

First, the four pigments. Chlorophyll a, bright or blue-green. Chlorophyll b, yellow-green. Xanthophylls, yellow. Carotenoids, yellow to yellow-orange. That list alone is not enough; you must order them.

The ordering rule is solubility. Carotenoids are the least polar of the four, so they are the most soluble in the running solvent, so they travel farthest and sit at the top. Their colour is yellow to yellow-orange. That is the answer.
Example four, high-difficulty assertion-reason. Read both statements slowly, because the whole item turns on whether the reason explains the assertion or merely sits beside it.
The assertion: in green plants, the oxygen evolved during photosynthesis comes from water. You already know this is true — van Niel proposed it and isotope work confirmed it.
The reason: photosynthetic sulphur bacteria use hydrogen sulphide instead of water and release sulphur rather than oxygen. Also true, straight from van Niel's own study organism.

Now the deciding question. Does the reason explain the assertion? Yes — completely. van Niel's whole argument was that analogy: if sulphur bacteria split hydrogen sulphide and deposit sulphur, then plants splitting water must release oxygen.

So the bacterial behaviour is not a coincidental true statement sitting nearby. It is precisely the evidence that led to the assertion. The answer is option (a): both true, and the reason explains the assertion.
दो और examples। तीसरा टेस्ट करता है कि तुम chromatogram पढ़ सकते हो या सिर्फ़ रटकर सुना सकते हो। चौथा वही assertion-reason है जो ये subtopic लगभग हर साल डालता है।

Example three, C U E T से: chromatogram पर चारों leaf pigments को arrange करो, और सबसे ऊपर पहुँचे, least-polar pigment का colour बताओ। ध्यान दो — सवाल ख़ुद reasoning tool दे रहा है, वो शब्द 'least-polar'।
पहले चारों pigments। Chlorophyll a — bright या blue-green। Chlorophyll b — yellow-green। Xanthophylls — yellow। Carotenoids — yellow से yellow-orange। सिर्फ़ ये list काफ़ी नहीं; इन्हें order करना है।

Order का rule है solubility। Carotenoids चारों में सबसे कम polar हैं, इसलिए running solvent में सबसे ज़्यादा soluble, इसलिए सबसे दूर तक चढ़ते हैं और सबसे ऊपर बैठते हैं। Colour — yellow से yellow-orange। यही answer है।
Example four, high-difficulty assertion-reason। दोनों statements आराम से पढ़ो, क्योंकि पूरा सवाल इसी पर टिका है कि reason assertion को समझा रहा है या बस बग़ल में खड़ा है।
Assertion: green plants में photosynthesis के दौरान निकलती oxygen water से आती है। ये तुम जानते हो कि सही है — van Niel ने propose किया और isotope work ने confirm किया।
Reason: photosynthetic sulphur bacteria water की जगह hydrogen sulphide use करते हैं और oxygen के बजाय sulphur छोड़ते हैं। ये भी सही — सीधे van Niel के अपने study organism से।

अब फ़ैसले वाला सवाल। क्या reason assertion को explain करता है? हाँ — पूरी तरह। van Niel की पूरी argument यही analogy थी: अगर sulphur bacteria hydrogen sulphide तोड़कर sulphur जमा करते हैं, तो water तोड़ते plants oxygen ही छोड़ेंगे।
यानी bacterial behaviour कोई इत्तेफ़ाक़न सही statement नहीं है जो पास खड़ा हो। वही evidence है जो assertion तक ले गया। Answer है option (a): दोनों true, और reason assertion को explain करता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: four traps this subtopic sets every year

board_events.text: Common student pitfalls
Trap 1: 'Oxygen comes from CO2.' It does not — it comes from water. The most-tested misconception in the chapter.
The 12-water-in / 6-water-out form of the overall equation is the giveaway.
Trap 2: mixing up absorption and action spectra. Absorption = what a pigment soaks up. Action = how fast photosynthesis runs. They overlap, but they are different graphs.
Trap 3: crediting the wrong scientist. Engelmann - action spectrum. van Niel - oxygen from water. Priestley - restored air. Ingenhousz - light and green parts.
Trap 4: thinking leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs green. The opposite — chlorophyll reflects green and absorbs blue and red.
Pro-tip: pin the unique pairs first
For scientist-matching, pin Engelmann's action spectrum and van Niel's water-source first; the remaining options sort themselves out by elimination.
Mnemonics: 'Pigs In Sachs's Engine, Never CO2' for the order. 'Blue and Red feed the plant; Green is sent back' for the wavelengths.

segments.text: Everything in this subtopic is straightforward the first time you read it, and then four specific traps quietly take marks off thousands of students. Let us name all four so they cannot catch you.

Trap one is the big one: believing the oxygen comes from carbon dioxide. It does not. It comes from water. This is the single most-tested misconception in the whole chapter, and it feels right, which is why it is so effective.
Your defence is the equation itself. Twelve waters in, six waters out. Nobody writes it that way by accident. If you can see that asymmetry, you can never be talked out of the correct answer.
Trap two is mixing up the two spectra. Absorption is what a pigment soaks up. Action is how fast photosynthesis runs. They overlap closely — and that overlap is exactly what makes them easy to blur.

Trap three is crediting the wrong scientist. Fix the four pairs and refuse to negotiate with them: Engelmann, action spectrum. van Niel, oxygen from water. Priestley, restored air. Ingenhousz, light and green parts.

Trap four is thinking leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs green. It is precisely the opposite. Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red, and reflects green back at you. The colour you see is the colour it rejected.
Now the pro-tip, and it is a technique rather than a fact. For any scientist-matching question, do not try to recall all four pairs at once under time pressure.

Pin the two most distinctive contributions first — Engelmann's action spectrum and van Niel's water-source. They have no competitors. Then the remaining options sort themselves out by elimination, far faster than recalling four cold.

<whisper>And two mnemonics for the last minute before the paper. 'Pigs In Sachs's Engine, Never C O two' gives you the scientists in order. 'Blue and Red feed the plant, Green is sent back' gives you the wavelengths.
इस subtopic में सब कुछ पहली बार पढ़ने में आसान लगता है — और फिर चार specific traps चुपचाप हज़ारों students के marks काट ले जाते हैं। चारों का नाम ले लेते हैं ताकि वो तुम्हें न पकड़ सकें।
Trap one सबसे बड़ा है: ये मानना कि oxygen carbon dioxide से आती है। नहीं आती। वो water से आती है। पूरे chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली misconception — और सही लगती है, इसीलिए इतनी ख़तरनाक है।
तुम्हारा बचाव ख़ुद equation है। बारह waters अंदर, छह बाहर। ऐसे कोई ग़लती से नहीं लिखता। ये asymmetry दिख गई तो कोई तुम्हें सही answer से हिला नहीं सकता।

Trap two है दोनों spectra को गड्डमड्ड करना। Absorption यानी pigment कितना सोखता है। Action यानी photosynthesis कितनी तेज़ चलती है। दोनों क़रीब-क़रीब overlap करते हैं — और यही overlap उन्हें आपस में मिला देता है।

Trap three है ग़लत scientist को credit देना। चारों pairs fix कर लो और इन पर कोई सौदेबाज़ी मत करो: Engelmann — action spectrum। van Niel — oxygen from water। Priestley — restored air। Ingenhousz — light और green parts।

Trap four है ये सोचना कि leaves हरी इसलिए हैं क्योंकि chlorophyll green सोखता है। बिलकुल उल्टा है। Chlorophyll blue और red सोखता है, और green वापस तुम्हारी तरफ़ फेंक देता है। जो रंग दिखता है, वही ठुकराया हुआ है।
अब pro-tip — ये fact नहीं, technique है। किसी भी scientist-matching question में time pressure के नीचे चारों pairs एक साथ याद करने की कोशिश मत करो।

पहले दो सबसे distinctive contributions pin करो — Engelmann का action spectrum और van Niel का water-source। इनका कोई competitor नहीं। फिर बाक़ी options elimination से ख़ुद settle हो जाते हैं, चारों रटने से कहीं तेज़।
<whisper>और paper से ठीक पहले वाले दो mnemonics। 'Pigs In Sachs's Engine, Never C O two' — scientists order में। 'Blue and Red feed the plant, Green is sent back' — wavelengths के लिए।

sections.title: The light reaction: two currencies and a two-stage booster

board_events.text: The light reaction: turning raw sunlight into usable currency
A plant cannot run on raw light, any more than a home can run directly on a lightning bolt. The light must be converted.
The currency comes in exactly two notes: ATP (energy) and NADPH (reducing power — a carrier loaded with high-energy electrons).
Inputs: light, water, and the pigment machinery. Famous by-product: oxygen.

board_events.caption: Two photons, two boosts: one electron carried from water all the way to NADPH

board_events.text: Light cannot lift an electron all the way to NADPH in a single jump. Plants use a two-stage booster — a relay race, not a single sprinter.
PS II catches a photon and kicks an electron up. It slides downhill through carriers, and that energy is banked as ATP.
PS I then catches a second photon and boosts the same electron again — high enough now to reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
The first electron comes from splitting water; the leftover oxygen is thrown away as exhaust. Plotted on an energy scale, this up-down-up trace looks like the letter Z.

segments.text: Think of a leaf as a tiny solar power station. Sunlight pours in for free — but a plant can no more run its machinery on raw light than your home can run directly on a lightning bolt.

The light has to be converted into a steady, usable currency. That conversion is the light reaction: the first of photosynthesis's two stages, and the part that actually captures sunlight and banks it as chemical energy.

The currency comes in exactly two notes. A T P, which is energy. And N A D P H, which is reducing power — a carrier loaded with high-energy electrons. Everything the plant builds later is paid for with these two.
To print them the plant needs three inputs: light, water, and the pigment machinery. And it produces one famous by-product — oxygen. The air you are breathing right now came out of this reaction.
Now the central trick, and this is where the marks are. Look at the energy scale in the figure and watch how the electron actually travels.
Light by itself cannot lift an electron all the way uphill to make N A D P H in one jump. So the plant uses a two-stage booster. Think relay race, not a single sprinter.
Photosystem two catches a photon first and kicks an electron up. That electron then slides downhill through a chain of carriers, and the energy released along the slide is banked as A T P.
Then Photosystem one catches a second photon and gives the very same electron a second kick — high enough, this time, to reduce N A D P plus into N A D P H. Two photons, two boosts, one electron.

And where does that first electron come from? From splitting water. The plant tears water apart to keep feeding fresh electrons into Photosystem two, and the leftover oxygen is simply thrown away as exhaust. Plot that up-down-up path and you get the letter Z.
Leaf को एक छोटा solar power station समझो। Sunlight मुफ़्त में बरस रही है — मगर plant raw light पर उतना ही नहीं चल सकता जितना तुम्हारा घर सीधे बिजली की कड़क पर।

Light को एक steady, usable currency में बदलना पड़ता है। यही conversion है light reaction: photosynthesis के दो stages में पहला, और वही हिस्सा जो असल में sunlight पकड़कर chemical energy में bank करता है।
Currency ठीक दो notes में आती है। A T P यानी energy। और N A D P H यानी reducing power — एक carrier जो high-energy electrons से लदा हुआ है। आगे plant जो भी बनाता है, इन्हीं दो से चुकाता है।
इन्हें छापने के लिए तीन inputs चाहिए: light, water, और pigment machinery। और निकलता है एक मशहूर by-product — oxygen। अभी तुम जो साँस ले रहे हो, वो इसी reaction से निकली है।
अब central trick, और marks यहीं हैं। Figure में energy scale देखो और ध्यान से देखो कि electron असल में सफ़र कैसे करता है।
अकेली light electron को एक ही jump में इतना ऊपर नहीं उठा सकती कि N A D P H बन जाए। इसलिए plant two-stage booster use करता है। Relay race सोचो, अकेला sprinter नहीं।
पहले Photosystem two एक photon पकड़ता है और electron को ऊपर उछाल देता है। फिर वो electron carriers की chain से नीचे फिसलता है, और उस फिसलन में निकली energy A T P में bank हो जाती है।
फिर Photosystem one दूसरा photon पकड़ता है और उसी electron को दूसरी kick देता है — इस बार इतनी ऊँची कि N A D P plus घटकर N A D P H बन जाए। दो photons, दो boosts, एक electron।

और वो पहला electron आता कहाँ से है? Water तोड़ने से। Plant पानी को फाड़कर Photosystem two में ताज़े electrons भेजता रहता है, और बची हुई oxygen exhaust की तरह बाहर फेंक दी जाती है। इस up-down-up रास्ते को plot करो — Z बन जाता है।

board_events.caption: Grana, stromal lamellae, thylakoid lumen and stroma

board_events.text: Inside the chloroplast, flattened sacs called thylakoids stack up into coin-pile structures called grana.
Long thylakoids connecting one granum to another are the stromal (inter-granal) lamellae.
The fluid matrix around all of them is the stroma. The interior space of a thylakoid is the lumen.
Light reaction → thylakoid membranes (grana). Dark reaction, the Calvin cycle → stroma.
Remember the lumen especially: the entire proton-gradient story is going to happen inside it.

segments.text: Before we follow the electron, we need the map. Location questions are free marks in C U E T and in the boards, and they are also the reason so many students misplace the Calvin cycle later.
The first thing to fix: the light reaction is membrane-bound. It does not float freely in the fluid of the chloroplast. It happens on a membrane, and that membrane has a very specific architecture.
Look at the chloroplast in section. Two envelope membranes on the outside, and inside, a whole internal world of green stacks sitting in a colourless fluid.
Those flattened sacs are thylakoids. Stacked one on another like a pile of coins, they form a granum — and a chloroplast holds many grana, which is where most of the green machinery lives.
Now look at the long tubes bridging one granum to the next. Those are the stromal lamellae, also called inter-granal lamellae. Keep them in mind — cyclic flow will turn out to prefer them.
The fluid matrix around all of this is the stroma. And the enclosed space inside a thylakoid — the hollow of the coin — is the lumen. Four words: granum, lamella, stroma, lumen.

Here is the line worth writing twice. Light reaction, on the thylakoid membranes of the grana. Dark reaction, the Calvin cycle, in the stroma. Two reactions, two addresses, and examiners will try to swap them.
And hold on to the lumen in particular. It looks like a boring empty space in the diagram. In two sections' time, that space fills with protons and becomes the reason A T P exists at all.
Electron के पीछे चलने से पहले हमें नक़्शा चाहिए। Location वाले सवाल C U E T और boards में free marks हैं — और यही वजह भी हैं कि आगे चलकर students Calvin cycle की जगह ग़लत बता देते हैं।
पहली बात पक्की कर लो: light reaction membrane-bound है। ये chloroplast के fluid में खुला तैर नहीं रही। ये एक membrane पर होती है, और उस membrane की architecture बहुत specific है।
Chloroplast को section में देखो। बाहर दो envelope membranes, और अंदर हरी stacks की पूरी एक दुनिया, एक रंगहीन fluid में बैठी हुई।
वो चपटी थैलियाँ thylakoids हैं। सिक्कों की ढेरी की तरह एक पर एक जमकर ये granum बनाती हैं — और एक chloroplast में कई grana होते हैं, जहाँ ज़्यादातर green machinery रहती है।
अब वो लंबी नलियाँ देखो जो एक granum को दूसरे से जोड़ती हैं। वो हैं stromal lamellae, जिन्हें inter-granal lamellae भी कहते हैं। इन्हें याद रखो — cyclic flow इन्हीं को पसंद करेगा।
इन सबके चारों तरफ़ का fluid matrix है stroma। और thylakoid के अंदर की बंद जगह — सिक्के का खोखलापन — वो है lumen। चार शब्द: granum, lamella, stroma, lumen।

अब वो line जो दो बार लिखने लायक़ है। Light reaction — grana की thylakoid membranes पर। Dark reaction यानी Calvin cycle — stroma में। दो reactions, दो पते, और examiners इन्हें आपस में बदलने की कोशिश करेंगे।
और ख़ासकर lumen पकड़े रहो। Diagram में ये एक बोरिंग खाली जगह लगती है। दो sections बाद यही जगह protons से भर जाएगी और A T P के होने की वजह बन जाएगी।

Accessory pigments: chlorophyll b, c and d, carotenoids and phycobilins.
They widen the range of usable wavelengths, funnel captured energy to chlorophyll a, and shield it from photo-oxidation.

board_events.caption: The antenna funnels energy inward to a single chlorophyll a at the reaction centre

board_events.text: Light Harvesting Complex (LHC): hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins in the thylakoid membrane — a satellite dish for photons.
Each photosystem = one LHC antenna + one reaction-centre chlorophyll a.
PS II — reaction centre P680 (absorption maximum near 680 nm). Does the photolysis of water and releases O2.
PS I — reaction centre P700 (near 700 nm). Hands the energised electron to NADP+, making NADPH. PS II acts FIRST despite carrying the higher number.

segments.text: We have the map. Now the machinery on it — and this section is where the single most-tested confusion in the chapter is born, so build it carefully.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment. It is the only pigment that sits at the reaction centre and directly drives the light reaction. It absorbs mainly in the violet-blue and the orange-red bands.
Everything else — chlorophyll b, c and d, the carotenoids, the phycobilins — is an accessory pigment. Accessory does not mean unimportant. It means supporting cast, with three specific jobs.
They widen the range of wavelengths the plant can use. They funnel the energy they capture to chlorophyll a. And they shield chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation, which is sun damage.
Now look at how that funnelling is physically arranged, because the geometry is the whole point of the design.

Hundreds of pigment molecules are bound to proteins and embedded in the thylakoid membrane. That assembly is the Light Harvesting Complex, the L H C, or antenna. It behaves like a satellite dish — collecting photons over a wide area and channelling that energy inward to one single chlorophyll a molecule, the reaction centre.

So write the definition tightly: each photosystem equals one antenna complex plus one reaction-centre chlorophyll a. Two photosystems means two antennas and two reaction centres, tuned slightly differently.
Photosystem two has the reaction centre P six eighty, named for its absorption maximum near six hundred eighty nanometres. Its job is the photolysis of water, and it is the one that releases oxygen.

Photosystem one has the reaction centre P seven hundred, near seven hundred nanometres. Its job is to hand the energised electron on to N A D P plus, making N A D P H. And note the trap now: Photosystem two acts first in the electron's journey, even though it carries the higher number.
नक़्शा मिल गया। अब उस पर की machinery — और chapter की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली confusion यहीं पैदा होती है, तो इसे ध्यान से बनाओ।
Chlorophyll a chief pigment है। यही अकेला pigment reaction centre पर बैठता है और सीधे light reaction चलाता है। ये मुख्यतः violet-blue और orange-red bands में absorb करता है।
बाक़ी सब — chlorophyll b, c, d, carotenoids, phycobilins — accessory pigments हैं। Accessory का मतलब बेकार नहीं। मतलब supporting cast, और उसके तीन तय काम।
ये plant के लिए wavelengths की range चौड़ी करते हैं। पकड़ी हुई energy को chlorophyll a तक funnel करते हैं। और chlorophyll a को photo-oxidation यानी sun damage से बचाते हैं।
अब देखो कि ये funnelling physically arrange कैसे की गई है — क्योंकि इस design का पूरा point यही geometry है।

सैकड़ों pigment molecules proteins से बँधे हुए thylakoid membrane में धँसे रहते हैं। उस पूरे assembly को कहते हैं Light Harvesting Complex, यानी L H C या antenna। ये satellite dish की तरह काम करता है — बड़े इलाक़े से photons बटोरकर उनकी energy अंदर, सिर्फ़ एक chlorophyll a molecule तक भेज देता है। वही reaction centre है।
तो definition कसकर लिखो: हर photosystem बराबर एक antenna complex plus एक reaction-centre chlorophyll a। दो photosystems यानी दो antennas और दो reaction centres, थोड़े अलग tune किए हुए।
Photosystem two का reaction centre है P six eighty, जो उसके absorption maximum — क़रीब छह सौ अस्सी nanometres — पर रखा गया नाम है। इसका काम है photolysis of water, और यही oxygen छोड़ता है।

Photosystem one का reaction centre है P seven hundred, क़रीब सात सौ nanometres पर। इसका काम है energised electron को N A D P plus तक पहुँचाना, यानी N A D P H बनाना। और trap अभी नोट कर लो: electron के सफ़र में Photosystem two पहले काम करता है, नंबर बड़ा होने के बावजूद।

board_events.caption: Up on a photon, down through carriers, up again, down to NADPH

board_events.text: 1. Antenna capture: photons strike the LHC pigments of PS II; the energy is funnelled to the P680 reaction centre.
2. First boost: P680 is excited and ejects a high-energy electron to a primary acceptor. P680 is now electron-hungry (oxidised).
3. Photolysis of water refills PS II: $2\,H_2O \rightarrow 4\,H^+ + 4\,e^- + O_2$
Electrons refill P680; the protons are dumped inside the thylakoid lumen; the oxygen is released as waste.
Direction of supply: water reduces PS II, PS II reduces PS I, PS I reduces NADP+ — an open chain, hence 'non-cyclic'.
4. Downhill slide = ATP: the electron travels down through plastoquinone → a cytochrome complex → plastocyanin, and the released energy is used to build ATP.
5. Second boost: plastocyanin delivers the electron to P700; a second photon re-excites it high enough.
6. NADPH formation: from PS I the electron passes via ferredoxin to NADP+ reductase, which reduces NADP+ to NADPH using an H+ from the stroma.

segments.text: Now we walk the electron from water to N A D P H, one step at a time. Six steps. If you can narrate these six in order, you can answer almost anything this subtopic asks.

Read the axis first, because the whole diagram depends on it. Vertical is redox potential, drawn so that more negative — higher energy — is further up. The two vertical jumps are photons. Everything sloping downward is the electron losing energy usefully.

Step one, antenna capture. Photons strike the L H C pigments of Photosystem two. The accessory pigments hand that energy inward, molecule to molecule, until it arrives at the P six eighty reaction centre.

Step two, the first boost. P six eighty absorbs that energy, gets excited, and ejects a high-energy electron to a primary acceptor. And now notice P six eighty's problem — it has given away an electron, so it is oxidised, electron-hungry, and it cannot fire again until it is refilled.
Step three solves that problem, and it is the famous one: photolysis of water. Two water molecules are split into four protons, four electrons, and one oxygen molecule.

Track all three products. The electrons refill P six eighty, so the photosystem can fire again. The protons are dumped inside the thylakoid lumen — remember that, it matters enormously in two sections. And the oxygen is released as waste.

And note the direction of supply, because this is the sentence that makes the word non-cyclic mean something. Water reduces Photosystem two. Photosystem two reduces Photosystem one. Photosystem one reduces N A D P plus. Every donation is one-way. It is an open chain.

Step four, the downhill slide, and this is where A T P comes from. The electron travels down the redox scale through plastoquinone, then a cytochrome complex, then plastocyanin. Energy released along the way is used to build A T P. Those carriers, arranged in order of redox potential, are exactly what give the scheme its zig-zag shape.
Step five, the second boost. Plastocyanin delivers the tired electron to P seven hundred in Photosystem one, and a second photon re-excites it to a high enough energy to do the final job.

Step six. From Photosystem one the electron passes via ferredoxin to the enzyme N A D P reductase, which reduces N A D P plus to N A D P H, using a proton from the stroma. Both notes — A T P and N A D P H — are now printed.
अब electron को water से N A D P H तक, एक-एक क़दम चलाते हैं। छह steps। अगर ये छह क्रम से सुना सको, तो इस subtopic का लगभग कुछ भी हल हो जाएगा।

पहले axis पढ़ो, क्योंकि पूरा diagram उसी पर टिका है। Vertical है redox potential, ऐसे बनाया गया कि ज़्यादा negative — यानी ऊँची energy — ऊपर की तरफ़ हो। दोनों vertical jumps photons हैं। नीचे की तरफ़ ढलान का मतलब electron की energy का काम आना।

Step one — antenna capture। Photons Photosystem two के L H C pigments पर पड़ते हैं। Accessory pigments उस energy को molecule-दर-molecule अंदर सरकाते हैं, जब तक वो P six eighty reaction centre तक न पहुँच जाए।

Step two — पहला boost। P six eighty वो energy सोखकर excited होता है और एक high-energy electron primary acceptor को उछाल देता है। अब P six eighty की मुसीबत देखो — electron दे चुका है, यानी oxidised है, electron-hungry, और भरे बिना दोबारा fire नहीं कर सकता।
Step three वही मुसीबत हल करता है, और यही मशहूर वाला है: photolysis of water। दो water molecules टूटकर देते हैं चार protons, चार electrons, और एक oxygen molecule।

तीनों products को track करो। Electrons P six eighty को भर देते हैं, ताकि photosystem फिर fire कर सके। Protons thylakoid lumen के अंदर गिरा दिए जाते हैं — ये याद रखो, दो sections बाद ये बेहद अहम होगा। और oxygen waste की तरह छोड़ दी जाती है।

और supply की direction नोट करो, क्योंकि यही वाक्य non-cyclic शब्द को मतलब देता है। Water reduces Photosystem two। Photosystem two reduces Photosystem one। Photosystem one reduces N A D P plus। हर donation one-way है। यही open chain है।

Step four — downhill slide, और A T P यहीं से आती है। Electron redox scale पर नीचे उतरता है — plastoquinone, फिर cytochrome complex, फिर plastocyanin। रास्ते में निकली energy A T P बनाने में लगती है। यही carriers, redox potential के क्रम में लगे हुए, scheme को उसका zig-zag shape देते हैं।
Step five — दूसरा boost। Plastocyanin थके हुए electron को Photosystem one के P seven hundred तक पहुँचाता है, और दूसरा photon उसे इतना ऊपर उठा देता है कि आख़िरी काम हो सके।

Step six। Photosystem one से electron ferredoxin के रास्ते enzyme N A D P reductase तक जाता है, जो stroma से एक proton लेकर N A D P plus को N A D P H में बदल देता है। दोनों notes — A T P और N A D P H — अब छप चुके हैं।

board_events.caption: Open chain versus closed loop: the comparison examiners love

board_events.text: Working with PS I alone, the electron expelled from P700 travels through the carrier chain and returns to P700 — a closed loop.
Because water is never split, there is no O2 and no NADPH. The loop simply spins to mint extra ATP.
Non-cyclic: PS I and PS II; water → PS II → PS I → NADP+; water split; O2 released; ATP and NADPH made; mainly in the grana thylakoids.
Cyclic: PS I only; P700 → carriers → back to P700; no water split; no O2; no NADPH; ATP only; mainly in the stromal lamellae.
Light-reaction summary: $2\,H_2O + 2\,NADP^+ + n\,ADP + n\,P_i \xrightarrow{light,\ pigments} 2\,NADPH + 2\,H^+ + n\,ATP + O_2$
Photophosphorylation = synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light energy. The term and the cyclic/non-cyclic distinction are credited to Arnon.

segments.text: The route we just walked is the full route. But a plant does not always want the full route, and understanding why is what separates a two-mark answer from a four-mark answer.
Suppose the cell has plenty of N A D P H already, but is short of A T P. Running the whole non-cyclic chain would only pile up more N A D P H it cannot use. So the plant short-circuits the route.
Compare the two panels side by side. On the left, an open chain with a beginning and an end. On the right, a closed loop that goes nowhere and comes back.

In cyclic photophosphorylation the plant works with Photosystem one alone. The electron expelled from P seven hundred travels through the carrier chain and returns to P seven hundred. It ends where it started.

And every consequence follows from one fact: water is never split. No photolysis means no oxygen, and no oxygen means the classic exam statement 'cyclic flow releases oxygen' is simply false. No N A D P plus is reduced either, so no N A D P H. The loop spins purely to mint extra A T P.

Now the comparison examiners actually ask for. Non-cyclic: both photosystems; water to Photosystem two to Photosystem one to N A D P plus; water is split; oxygen released; both A T P and N A D P H made; and it happens mainly in the grana thylakoids.

Cyclic: Photosystem one only; P seven hundred through the carriers and back to P seven hundred; no water split; no oxygen; no N A D P H; A T P is the only product; and it happens mainly in the stromal lamellae. Notice A T P is the one row where both columns say yes.

The overall light-reaction summary, with water as the electron donor, gathers it into one line: two waters plus two N A D P plus plus A D P and inorganic phosphate, driven by light and pigments, give two N A D P H, protons, A T P, and oxygen.

And the term itself. Photophosphorylation means the synthesis of A T P from A D P and inorganic phosphate using light energy. Both the term and the cyclic-versus-non-cyclic distinction are credited to Arnon — a name worth two marks by itself.
अभी जो रास्ता हमने चला, वो पूरा रास्ता है। मगर plant को हमेशा पूरा रास्ता नहीं चाहिए — और यही समझना दो-marks वाले जवाब को चार-marks वाला बनाता है।
मान लो cell के पास N A D P H पहले से भरपूर है, मगर A T P कम है। पूरी non-cyclic chain चलाने से सिर्फ़ और N A D P H जमा होगा, जो काम ही नहीं आएगा। इसलिए plant रास्ता short-circuit कर देता है।
दोनों panels आमने-सामने देखो। बाईं तरफ़ open chain — शुरुआत भी, अंत भी। दाईं तरफ़ closed loop — कहीं जाता नहीं, घूमकर वापस आ जाता है।
Cyclic photophosphorylation में plant अकेले Photosystem one से काम चलाता है। P seven hundred से निकला electron carrier chain से गुज़रकर वापस P seven hundred पर आ जाता है। जहाँ से चला, वहीं ख़त्म।

और हर नतीजा एक ही बात से निकलता है: water कभी split होता ही नहीं। Photolysis नहीं तो oxygen नहीं, और oxygen नहीं तो exam का classic statement 'cyclic flow oxygen छोड़ता है' सीधा ग़लत। N A D P plus भी reduce नहीं होता, तो N A D P H भी नहीं। Loop सिर्फ़ extra A T P छापने के लिए घूमता है।

अब वो comparison जो examiners असल में माँगते हैं। Non-cyclic: दोनों photosystems; water से Photosystem two, फिर Photosystem one, फिर N A D P plus; water split होता है; oxygen निकलती है; A T P और N A D P H दोनों बनते हैं; और ये मुख्यतः grana thylakoids में होता है।

Cyclic: सिर्फ़ Photosystem one; P seven hundred से carriers होते हुए वापस P seven hundred; water split नहीं; oxygen नहीं; N A D P H नहीं; सिर्फ़ A T P; और ये मुख्यतः stromal lamellae में। ध्यान दो — A T P अकेली row है जहाँ दोनों columns हाँ कहते हैं।

Overall light-reaction summary, water को electron donor मानकर, सब एक line में समेट देती है: दो water plus दो N A D P plus plus A D P और inorganic phosphate, light और pigments से चलकर, देते हैं दो N A D P H, protons, A T P, और oxygen।

और ख़ुद term। Photophosphorylation यानी light energy से A D P और inorganic phosphate से A T P बनाना। ये term और cyclic बनाम non-cyclic का फ़र्क़, दोनों का credit जाता है Arnon को — अकेले दो marks लायक़ नाम।

board_events.caption: Three sources load the lumen with protons; one gate lets them out

board_events.text: Source 1: water splitting happens on the inner (lumen) side, releasing H+ directly inside.
Source 2: as electrons move through the chain, plastoquinone physically ferries H+ from the stroma across to the lumen.
Source 3: NADP+ reduction removes an H+ from the stroma side.
Result: many protons trapped inside the lumen, few outside — a steep difference, like water held behind a dam.
One gate only: ATP synthase — F0 channel in the membrane, F1 head facing the stroma. Protons gush through F0, the enzyme spins like a turbine, and ADP + Pi are forced together into ATP.
Classic proof: isolated thylakoids made acidic inside (lumen pH 4) and dropped into an alkaline bath (pH 8) in the DARK still make ATP. Energy lives in the gradient, not in light directly.

segments.text: We said the downhill slide is banked as A T P. But that phrase hides the mechanism, and the mechanism is exactly what a four-mark question asks for. So: how does a membrane actually make A T P?

Not by magic as the electron slides down. The energy of the slide is spent on one thing only — pushing protons across the thylakoid membrane, piling them up on one side. That imbalance is the real product.
Picture a dam on a hill river. The membrane is the dam wall. The lumen is the reservoir. And the electron chain is the monsoon, quietly filling the reservoir higher and higher.

Three things crowd protons into the lumen. Source one: water splitting happens on the inner, lumen side of the membrane, so it releases its protons directly inside. You already met those four protons in the Z-scheme.
Source two: as electrons move through the chain, the carrier plastoquinone physically ferries protons from the stroma across to the lumen. It does not just pass electrons — it carries hydrogen.

Source three is the subtle one, and it works from the other side. Reducing N A D P plus to N A D P H consumes a proton from the stroma. Removing protons from outside steepens the gradient just as surely as adding them inside.

The result: many protons trapped inside the lumen, few outside. A steep concentration difference — water held high behind a dam wall. And the membrane is watertight to protons everywhere except one place.

That one gate is the enzyme A T P synthase. Its F zero channel is embedded in the membrane; its F one head faces the stroma. As protons gush through F zero, the enzyme spins like a turbine in a hydroelectric dam, and that mechanical turning forces A D P and inorganic phosphate together into A T P.

<excited>And here is the experiment that proves the whole idea. Take isolated thylakoids, make the lumen acidic — p H four — then drop them into an alkaline bath at p H eight, in total darkness. They still make A T P. No light at all. The energy was never in the light; it was in the gradient.
हमने कहा था कि downhill slide A T P में bank होती है। मगर वो वाक्य mechanism छिपा देता है — और चार-marks वाला सवाल यही mechanism माँगता है। तो: membrane असल में A T P बनाती कैसे है?
जादू से नहीं, कि electron फिसला और A T P बन गई। उस फिसलन की energy सिर्फ़ एक काम में लगती है — protons को thylakoid membrane के पार धकेलना, एक तरफ़ ढेर लगाना। वही असली product है।
पहाड़ी नदी पर बना dam सोचो। Membrane dam की दीवार है। Lumen reservoir है। और electron chain monsoon है, जो चुपचाप reservoir को ऊँचा और ऊँचा भरती जा रही है।
तीन चीज़ें lumen में protons ठूँसती हैं। Source one: water splitting membrane की अंदरूनी, lumen वाली तरफ़ होती है, इसलिए उसके protons सीधे अंदर ही गिरते हैं। Z-scheme वाले वही चार protons याद हैं ना।
Source two: जैसे electrons chain से गुज़रते हैं, carrier plastoquinone protons को stroma से उठाकर lumen तक ले जाता है। ये सिर्फ़ electrons pass नहीं करता — hydrogen ढोता है।

Source three सूक्ष्म है और दूसरी तरफ़ से काम करता है। N A D P plus को N A D P H में बदलने में stroma का एक proton ख़र्च होता है। बाहर से protons हटाना gradient को उतना ही तीखा करता है जितना अंदर डालना।

नतीजा: lumen के अंदर ढेरों protons फँसे हुए, बाहर बहुत कम। एक steep concentration difference — dam की दीवार के पीछे ऊँचा चढ़ा पानी। और membrane protons के लिए हर जगह watertight है, सिर्फ़ एक जगह छोड़कर।

वो अकेला gate है enzyme A T P synthase। इसका F zero channel membrane में धँसा है; F one head stroma की तरफ़ है। जैसे ही protons F zero से बहते हैं, enzyme hydroelectric dam की turbine की तरह घूमता है, और वही घुमाव A D P और inorganic phosphate को जोड़कर A T P बना देता है।

<excited>और अब वो experiment जो पूरा idea साबित करता है। Isolated thylakoids लो, lumen को acidic बनाओ — p H four — फिर उन्हें p H eight वाले alkaline bath में डाल दो, पूरे अँधेरे में। वो फिर भी A T P बनाते हैं। Light बिलकुल नहीं। Energy कभी light में थी ही नहीं; वो gradient में थी।

board_events.text: Depth note: why two photosystems?

board_events.text: He also found that shining two wavelengths together produced more than the sum of each alone — the Enhancement Effect.
The clean explanation: two cooperating photosystems, absorbing at slightly different peaks, must BOTH be driven for full non-cyclic flow.
Honest caveat 1: the light reaction needs light, full stop. Switch off the lamp and it stops within moments.
Honest caveat 2: the 'oxygen is released' story is true only for non-cyclic flow. Cyclic mode makes extra ATP but no NADPH and no oxygen.
Honest caveat 3: this is plant and cyanobacterial behaviour. Some photosynthetic bacteria use a single photosystem, never split water, and release no oxygen.

segments.text: <curious>Step back and ask an awkward question. Two photosystems, two antennas, two reaction centres — why would evolution build all that when one might do? The answer came from an anomaly nobody could explain.

Emerson found that photosynthesis falls off sharply beyond about six hundred eighty nanometres. That should not happen. Chlorophyll still absorbs light out there — the pigment is working, but the process is not. This is the Red Drop.
Look at the curve, then at the bars. The curve is the anomaly. The bars are the clue that cracked it.

Emerson then shone two wavelengths together — one shorter red, one longer red. Each alone gave a modest rate. Both together gave more than the sum of the two rates added up. Not equal to the sum. More than it. That is the Enhancement Effect.

The clean explanation is the one you have been learning all subtopic. There are two cooperating photosystems, absorbing at slightly different peaks, and both must be driven for full non-cyclic flow. Feed only one and the relay stalls; feed both and it runs.

Now three honest caveats to keep your statements exam-proof. First: the light reaction needs light, full stop. Switch off the lamp and it stops within moments. The Calvin cycle can coast briefly on stored A T P and N A D P H, but it soon stops too.

Second: the oxygen-is-released story is true only for non-cyclic flow. In cyclic mode the plant runs Photosystem one alone, mints extra A T P, and makes no N A D P H and no oxygen. Never say 'photosynthesis always releases oxygen' without that qualifier.

Third: all of this is plant and cyanobacterial behaviour. Some photosynthetic bacteria use a single photosystem, never split water, and therefore release no oxygen at all — the exception examiners love, and the same exception that gave van Niel his answer.

<curious>ज़रा पीछे हटकर एक असहज सवाल पूछो। दो photosystems, दो antennas, दो reaction centres — evolution ये सब क्यों बनाएगा जब एक से काम चल सकता था? जवाब एक ऐसी anomaly से आया जो किसी को समझ नहीं आ रही थी।

Emerson ने पाया कि क़रीब छह सौ अस्सी nanometres के आगे photosynthesis तेज़ी से गिर जाती है। ऐसा होना नहीं चाहिए। Chlorophyll वहाँ अब भी light absorb करता है — pigment काम कर रहा है, process नहीं। यही है Red Drop।
पहले curve देखो, फिर bars। Curve anomaly है। Bars वो clue हैं जिन्होंने इसे तोड़ा।

फिर Emerson ने दो wavelengths एक साथ डालीं — एक छोटी red, एक लंबी red। अकेले-अकेले दोनों ने मामूली rate दी। दोनों साथ में — दोनों rates के जोड़ से भी ज़्यादा। जोड़ के बराबर नहीं। उससे ज़्यादा। यही Enhancement Effect है।

साफ़ explanation वही है जो तुम पूरे subtopic से सीख रहे हो। दो cooperating photosystems हैं, थोड़े अलग peaks पर absorb करते हैं, और full non-cyclic flow के लिए दोनों को चलाना ज़रूरी है। सिर्फ़ एक को खिलाओ तो relay अटक जाती है; दोनों को खिलाओ तो चलती है।

अब तीन ईमानदार caveats, ताकि तुम्हारे statements exam-proof रहें। पहला: light reaction को light चाहिए, बस। Lamp बंद करो, पल भर में रुक जाती है। Calvin cycle stored A T P और N A D P H पर थोड़ी देर coast कर लेती है, मगर वो भी जल्दी रुक जाती है।

दूसरा: oxygen निकलने वाली कहानी सिर्फ़ non-cyclic flow के लिए सच है। Cyclic mode में plant अकेला Photosystem one चलाता है, extra A T P छापता है, और N A D P H भी नहीं बनाता और oxygen भी नहीं। बिना इस qualifier के मत कहो कि photosynthesis हमेशा oxygen छोड़ती है।

तीसरा: ये सब plants और cyanobacteria का behaviour है। कुछ photosynthetic bacteria अकेला photosystem use करते हैं, water कभी split नहीं करते, इसलिए oxygen बिलकुल नहीं छोड़ते — वही exception जो examiners को प्यारा है, और वही जिसने van Niel को जवाब दिया था।

sections.title: Worked examples: differentiating the two pathways, and the electron's final destination

board_events.text: Example 1 [CBSE Board]: differentiate cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
(a) Photosystems: cyclic uses PS I only; non-cyclic uses both PS I and PS II.
(b) Oxygen: cyclic involves no photolysis of water, so no O2. Non-cyclic splits water, so O2 is evolved.
(c) Products: cyclic forms only ATP; non-cyclic forms ATP and NADPH (plus O2).
Concluding line: non-cyclic flow supplies both energy and reducing power for the Calvin cycle; cyclic flow tops up ATP alone.
Example 2 [NEET Speed Trap]: where do the electrons from photolysis end up?

board_events.text: Options: (a) glucose (b) ATP (c) water (d) NADPH. Do not overthink the path: water → PS II → PS I → NADP+.
Answer: (d) NADPH. Speed line: the light reaction's electron always dies in NADPH; carbon's electron later dies in sugar.

segments.text: Two examples, two very different skills. The first is a board answer where structure earns the marks. The second is a speed trap where the wrong answer is the one that feels most impressive.
Example one, C B S E: differentiate cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation on three bases. Answer on exactly the bases asked, in the order asked — that structure alone is worth marks.
Basis (a), photosystems. Cyclic uses Photosystem one only. Non-cyclic uses both Photosystem one and Photosystem two. One line, no hedging.

Basis (b), oxygen. Cyclic involves no photolysis of water, so no oxygen is evolved. Non-cyclic splits water, so oxygen is evolved. Notice the answer gives the cause and then the consequence — that is what an examiner is reading for.

Basis (c), products. Cyclic forms only A T P. Non-cyclic forms A T P and N A D P H, plus the oxygen. Then close with a concluding line: non-cyclic flow supplies both energy and reducing power for the Calvin cycle, while cyclic flow tops up A T P alone.
Example two, a N E E T speed trap. The electrons released by the photolysis of water during non-cyclic flow ultimately end up in — glucose, A T P, water, or N A D P H?
Follow the arrows and do not improvise. Water, to Photosystem two, to Photosystem one, to N A D P plus. The chain ends there. The electron's final resting place in the light reaction is N A D P H.

Now see why glucose is so tempting. It feels like the grand final answer of the whole chapter. But glucose is made later, in the Calvin cycle — that is the trap. A T P is energised by the electron's journey, not its destination. And water is the source, not the sink.
So the answer is option (d), N A D P H. And carry the speed line out of here: the light reaction's electron always dies in N A D P H; carbon's electron later dies in sugar.
दो examples, दो बिलकुल अलग skills। पहला board answer है जहाँ structure marks दिलाता है। दूसरा speed trap है जहाँ ग़लत answer ही सबसे impressive लगता है।
Example one, C B S E: cyclic और non-cyclic photophosphorylation में तीन basis पर फ़र्क़ बताओ। ठीक उन्हीं basis पर, उसी order में जवाब दो — ये structure ही अपने आप में marks है।
Basis (a), photosystems। Cyclic सिर्फ़ Photosystem one use करता है। Non-cyclic दोनों — Photosystem one और Photosystem two। एक line, कोई गोलमोल नहीं।

Basis (b), oxygen। Cyclic में photolysis of water होती ही नहीं, इसलिए oxygen नहीं। Non-cyclic water तोड़ता है, इसलिए oxygen निकलती है। ध्यान दो — जवाब पहले cause देता है, फिर consequence। Examiner यही पढ़ रहा होता है।

Basis (c), products। Cyclic सिर्फ़ A T P बनाता है। Non-cyclic बनाता है A T P और N A D P H, साथ में oxygen। फिर concluding line से बंद करो: non-cyclic flow Calvin cycle को energy और reducing power दोनों देता है, जबकि cyclic flow सिर्फ़ A T P top-up करता है।
Example two, N E E T speed trap। Non-cyclic flow में photolysis of water से निकले electrons आख़िरकार कहाँ पहुँचते हैं — glucose, A T P, water, या N A D P H?
Arrows के पीछे चलो, अपनी तरफ़ से मत जोड़ो। Water, फिर Photosystem two, फिर Photosystem one, फिर N A D P plus। Chain वहीं ख़त्म। Light reaction में electron का आख़िरी ठिकाना है N A D P H।

अब देखो glucose इतना lubhavna क्यों लगता है। वो पूरे chapter का grand final answer महसूस होता है। मगर glucose बाद में बनता है, Calvin cycle में — यही trap है। A T P electron के सफ़र से energised होती है, वो उसकी मंज़िल नहीं। और water source है, sink नहीं।
तो answer है option (d), N A D P H। और ये speed line साथ ले जाओ: light reaction का electron हमेशा N A D P H में मरता है; carbon का electron बाद में sugar में मरता है।

sections.title: Worked examples: spotting the reversed statement, and a weedicide that blocks the chain

board_events.text: Example 3 [CUET]: which statement about non-cyclic photophosphorylation is INCORRECT?

(a) Water is oxidised in PS II but not in PS I. (b) Photons are needed to activate both PS I and PS II. (c) Photolysis of water and formation of ATP + NADPH occur. (d) Production of NADPH is associated with PS II, not PS I.
Answer: (d) — it reverses the roles. NADPH is produced at PS I; PS II's job is water-splitting.
Example 4 [NEET High-Difficulty]: a weedicide blocks electron transport from PS II to PS I
